name: The Strangler Figs of the Key West Cemetery

location.address: Historic Key West City Cemetery, Old Town, Key West, FL

verified_sources: https://www.keysnews.com/news/local/city-tree-commission-postpones-decision-on-cemetery-trees-indefinitely/article_34109605-dc00-4558-9ddf-97e7a4051d10.html (Keys Weekly/Keys News, Feb 2026, quoting the City urban forestry report)
access: Free. City-owned historic cemetery in Old Town, open to walk through (hours not fetched; writer must not invent any).
transport: Old Town Key West at the foot of Solares Hill; walkable from the Old Town streets (no transit stop verified).
verify_notes: ONE source family (local press quoting the City's own Urban Forestry report), flagged. The report by Urban Forestry Manager Brett Mayle and Assistant Zach Bentley measured two strangler figs at 96 inches and 53 inches DIAMETER. girth_cm 766 is pi x 96 in (243.8 cm), the larger tree; the second would be about 423 cm. The articles do not say how high the diameters were taken. Species given only as 'strangler figs' (Ficus aurea is the native strangler of the Keys but no source names it here), so genus only. The report shows the figs deeply intertwined with gravestones, breaking slabs or engulfing them. A resident's letter says most graves beneath them date to the 1880s; the cemetery was founded in 1847 after the 1846 hurricane. 'Over century-old' is the paper's wording, no planting date. THE CITY URBAN FORESTERS ASKED TO REMOVE BOTH TREES (item on the Tree Commission agenda since Nov 2025; residents wrote letters of opposition; the Nov 10 meeting was cancelled for lack of quorum, then staff requested indefinite postponement). No decision found as of the last article. A writer must say the trees are under a removal request; before publishing re-check keywest.legistar.com Tree Commission agendas for a removal vote. Alive check: lifecheck RECENT 2025-05-15 is an unrelated iNaturalist observation nearby, not these trees. Exact position inside the 19-acre cemetery NOT found (agenda attachments on keywest.legistar.com not fetched); pin is the cemetery centre, approximate, not a small site. Twin trees: two figs reported, distance apart unknown, delivered as one collectible point only if they stand near each other; otherwise the larger alone.
story:
Key West's own urban foresters have asked to cut these two trees down. The strangler figs in the city cemetery have grown so deep into the graves that the city's forestry report shows them breaking slabs and engulfing headstones, and in November 2025 removing both went on the Tree Commission's agenda.

The report, by Brett Mayle and Zach Bentley of the city's urban forestry team, measured them at 96 and 53 inches across, about 2.4 and 1.35 metres. Worked out as a circle, which a strangler fig's trunk never quite is, the larger comes to roughly 7.7 metres round. It does not say how high up the trunk the tape went.

The local paper calls them over a century old; there is no planting date. The cemetery was founded in 1847, after the hurricane of 1846, and a resident wrote to the commission that most of the graves beneath the figs date from the 1880s.

Residents wrote in against it.The November meeting was cancelled for lack of a quorum, and by February 2026 city staff had asked for the decision to be postponed indefinitely. That is the last word we have found: no vote, and the figs still standing among the stones.

No source names the species, so we give only the genus, and none says where in the 19-acre cemetery they stand, or how far apart. Our pin is the cemetery's middle, in Old Town. Entry is free. If you find them, tell us where.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by what they are doing to the graves: two strangler figs grown into the headstones, the larger about 2.4 metres across. They stand somewhere inside the Key West Cemetery in Old Town.

name: The Kapok Tree

location.address: Whitehead Street at Jackson Square (marked 502 Whitehead St), Key West, FL 33040

access: Free, street-side lawn on Whitehead Street beside the courthouse; a white sign marks the spot.
verify_notes: Pin: OSM natural=tree node 9395545457 named 'The Kapok Tree' (24.5547564,-81.8038174); the OSM address point 502 Whitehead St sits about 40 m north, so the pin is the tree node, not the address. Age: WLRN (2024-04-01, courthouse hardening story) says 'In 1900, a kapok tree was planted at Jackson Square. The giant, beautiful tree still stands today and draws people in for photos daily' and that it will not be disturbed by construction. Florida Keys tourism board (Whitehead Street walk page): trunk circumference 'more than 30 feet' (girth_cm 914 is that figure, a lower bound; buttressed trunk), 'estimated to be more than 100 years old', 'one of the country's most famous Kapok trees', pink and white flowers spring and summer, a sign marks the spot. A search summary claimed a 2018 survey dates it 1905; that PDF (williamvdavidson.com, The Kapoks of Key West 2018) could not be read, so it is NOT used; 1900 vs 1905 is an unresolved possible discrepancy. Alive: lifecheck RECENT, iNaturalist observation 2026-11-10 at the pin (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/414403808). Two sources plus OSM. Same walk as kyw_004 (about 250 m).
story:
The trunk of the Kapok Tree on Whitehead Street measures more than 30 feet around, and with its buttresses that figure is a floor, not a ceiling. It stands on the lawn at Jackson Square beside Monroe County's historic courthouse, and a white sign marks the spot, in case the size does not.

Its birth year depends on who you ask. WLRN, reporting in 2024, says a kapok was planted at Jackson Square in 1900. Another account puts the planting at 1905, but we could not read that survey ourselves, so treat those five years as an open question. Either way, the Florida Keys tourism board's estimate of more than a hundred years holds.

It has spent that century next to the county's courthouse. When WLRN reported on the work to harden the old building against hurricanes, it noted that the construction would not disturb the tree. The station also says it draws people in for photographs every day, and the tourism board calls it one of the country's most famous kapoks.

Come in spring or summer and the crown carries pink and white flowers. The rest of the year the trunk does the talking on its own. If you know for certain whether it went into the ground in 1900 or 1905, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the buttressed trunk, more than 30 feet round, and the white sign that marks it. It stands on the lawn at Jackson Square, beside the courthouse on Whitehead Street.

name: The Cosgrove House Banyan

location.address: 323 Whitehead Street (front yard of the Cosgrove House, Banyan Resort), Key West, FL 33040

access: View-only from the public sidewalk on Whitehead Street; the yard belongs to the Banyan Resort, a private hotel. Do not enter the property.

location_site.name: Cosgrove House front yard, 323 Whitehead St

verify_notes: Age: Key West Historic Marker Tour (marker at 323 Whitehead, page copyright 2018): the house is 'literally overshadowed by a landscaping decision Myrtle Cosgrove, the Captain's wife, made a century ago'; she planted a banyan for shade when Key West was not lush and fresh water came from cisterns. The Banyan Resort's own history page: the front yard contains 'one of the two expansive Banyan Trees on this property which was planted in the early 1900s by Captain Cosgrove's wife, Myrtle'; a second, 'the largest Banyan Tree on the property', stands in the gardens behind (not assessed). The two sources agree on planting by Myrtle Cosgrove in the early 1900s (the resort is the owner of the ground; the marker tour is independent). Species given only as 'banyan' (a strangling fig, genus Ficus), not narrowed. Alive: lifecheck RECENT, iNaturalist observation 2026-05-31 near the address (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/367213402). Pin is the OSM address point for 323 Whitehead, not the trunk; stays approximate; small-site rule (hotel front yard seen from the street). No girth or height found. About 250 m from the Kapok Tree.
story:
A captain's wife planted this banyan for shade, and a century later it overshadows her house. Myrtle Cosgrove, wife of Captain Cosgrove, put it in the front yard of 323 Whitehead Street in the early 1900s, at a time when Key West was not lush and fresh water came out of cisterns.

The Key West Historic Marker Tour says without softening that the Cosgrove House is literally overshadowed by a landscaping decision she made a hundred years ago. The Banyan Resort, which owns the house today, tells the same story of the planting on its own history page, and adds that this is one of two expansive banyans on the property. The other, which the resort calls the largest, grows in the gardens behind, out of sight from the street.

Neither source names the species beyond banyan, a strangling fig of the genus Ficus, so that is how we list it. Nobody has published its girth or its height either. If you have measured it, or know which fig it is, tell us.

This one is a tree to look at, not to walk under. The yard belongs to a private hotel, so stand on the public sidewalk of Whitehead Street and look in rather than stepping onto the grounds. The Kapok Tree at Jackson Square is about 250 metres away, which makes the two an easy pair on one short walk.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the banyan in the front yard of the Cosgrove House, 323 Whitehead Street, seen from the public sidewalk. The resort's larger banyan stands in the back gardens, out of view.
